extracted.intended_audience: press-release writers, PR professionals, small-business owners and communications staff preparing press releases for media
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting press releases that follow Associated Press (AP) Style and newsroom conventions so releases are concise, media-ready, and more likely to be used by editors. Covers structure (headline, lead, boilerplate, contact) and specific AP rules for language, punctuation, capitalization, and numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key elements of an AP Style press release
rubrics_metrics.description: An AP Style Press Release is a press release that follows the guidelines of the Associated Press (AP) Stylebook. Key elements include a compelling headline, dateline, introductory paragraph (the lead), body text, boilerplate, and contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These structural elements make the release easy for editors to scan and convert into a story; ensure each element is present and clearly labeled (dateline, boilerplate, contact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate the message in the first sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate the Message of Your Press Release in the First Sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set your goal in the beginning—if the editor reads the first line or two without finding the objective of the release, they’re likely to discard it. The lead should state the main point immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover the Five Ws
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover the Five Ws in the Body of Your Press Release: who, what, where, when and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once you have an editor’s attention, deliver the payoff by supplying all the information needed to write a full story so editors don’t have to dig for details on tight deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliver clear, concise, and accurate information
rubrics_metrics.description: This style is designed to deliver clear, concise, and accurate information about an organization’s news or announcements to media outlets and journalists, while ensuring consistency and credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AP rules for language use so your news is easily understood and readily usable by media; avoid unnecessary jargon or fluff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AP Style rules for punctuation, abbreviation, capitalization, and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: By following the AP Stylebook’s specific rules for language use such as punctuation, abbreviation, capitalization, and numbers, organizations can ensure their news is easily understood and readily usable for media purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to AP conventions across these categories to meet editors' expectations and improve pickup rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never use two spaces after a punctuation mark
rubrics_metrics.description: Never Use Two Spaces After a Punctuation Mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only one space after punctuation—none before. (This may require changing habits if you were taught to type with two spaces after sentences.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AP (serial) comma rules — drop the final Oxford comma
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Serial Comma Formatting Rather Than Oxford Commas. When following AP Style, drop the last comma in a series (i.e., do not use the Oxford comma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast given: 'I ate bananas, peanut butter and chocolate.' Ensure consistency with AP practice throughout the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use full names and titles on first reference only
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Full Names and Titles the First Time You Introduce Someone; leave them off after that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On first introduction give a person’s full name and title (e.g., CEO). After that, use only the last name to avoid clunky repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numbers according to AP number rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Numbers Correctly. Spell out numbers between one and nine; use numerals for 10 and above. Also use numbers for dates and abbreviate months with more than five letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AP conventions for numerals vs. spelled-out numbers, dates, and month abbreviations to meet editorial style expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use title case in headings and subheadings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Title Case Capitalization in Headings and Subheadings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title case capitalizes the first letter of every word except articles (a, an, the), coordinating conjunctions (and, or, but…), and short prepositions (in, on, for…). Note that a word’s role can change whether it’s capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make releases editor-ready to increase pickup
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors expect releases to follow AP style and be easy to convert into stories; adherence increases the chance they will pick up your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play by editors' rules—accuracy, brevity, correct style—so your release will be accepted rather than discarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate must succinctly describe the organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a boilerplate as one of the key elements: a short paragraph that succinctly describes the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep boilerplate consistent across releases and concise so reporters can copy standard language about the issuer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include clear contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Include contact information as a key element so media can reach a representative for follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a named contact, phone number, email and any relevant availability to facilitate journalist follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelling headline and dateline
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a compelling headline and an appropriate dateline as structural elements of the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headline should summarize the news and entice the editor; dateline should indicate location and date to orient the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead (introductory paragraph) should function as a journalistic lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory paragraph (the lead) should present the most important facts up front and answer primary questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the lead like a journalist would, prioritizing the most newsworthy information in the first paragraph.
